title: PrivAct: Internalizing Contextual Privacy Preservation via Multi-Agent Preference Training
pdf_path: papers/PrivAct_Internalizing Contextual Privacy Preservation via Multi-Agent Preference Training.pdf
threat_model_summary: Main experiments assume benign instructions but contextually inappropriate disclosure; no adaptive attacker except one Qwen3-32B compositional attack in Appendix D.5. Defense is training-time preference alignment, not a runtime reference monitor.
core_contributions: Internalizes contextual privacy into generator/verifier/refiner agents via multi-agent preference training
Tree-structured generation with descendant-averaged credit assignment for intermediate agents
LC-ARS reward that makes privacy a precondition for helpfulness reward
Reports up to 12.32 percentage-point leakage reduction with comparable helpfulness across four backbones and six topologies
limitations: No attacker in main experiments; only one compositional attack in D.5
12.32% is percentage points and a Mistral-specific operating point, not a universal relative reduction
Verifier still produces explicit privacy critiques at inference; trace may leak sensitive items
Only verifier/refiner fine-tuning is evidenced; 'each agent' claim is not fully supported
No confidence intervals or significance tests; judge absolute scores differ by an order of magnitude across judges
Closed-source models cannot be directly fine-tuned
theoretical_crypto_links: None; contextual integrity is a normative theory, not a formal privacy definition
L is an LLM-judge disclosure rate, not differential privacy, QIF, or a cryptographic leakage bound
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, credentials, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed context credentials and tool-boundary capability tokens are our inference, not the paper's mechanism
evidence_refs: pp.1-4 problem, tree generation, reward, DPO
p.7 topology results and component ablation
pp.15-20 appendices C-E, including training details and compositional attack

title: From Weak Cues to Real Identities: Evaluating Inference-Driven De-Anonymization in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/From Weak Cues to Real Identities_Evaluating Inference-Driven De-Anonymization in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: An analyst or LLM agent is authorized to access an anonymized dataset plus auxiliary public or private sources, and reconstructs a real identity by combining weak cues. The failure is inference/use, not unauthorized access; no cryptographic adversary or formal anonymity notion is modeled.
core_contributions: Defines inference-driven linkage as an agent privacy failure mode
Builds InferLink, a controlled benchmark varying fingerprint type, task intent, and attacker knowledge
Evaluates classical Netflix/AOL linkage, InferLink, and human-AI interaction traces under one interface
Shows GPT-5 reconstructs 79.17% of Netflix identities at m=2 versus 56.0-60.2% for classical baselines
Shows a privacy-aware prompt can suppress explicit linkage but causes large utility loss and is not a formal guarantee
limitations: InferLink has only 20 binary samples per cell and 60 unique pairs; no confidence intervals or significance tests
Synthetic 10x9 schema and single ground-truth overlap limit external validity
Case studies cannot estimate incidence and are selected for linkability
LSR is binary and ignores wrong-but-confident identities and partial anonymity-set shrinkage
Prompt defense is a soft constraint, tested without adaptive paraphrasing or task decomposition
No comparison with differential privacy, k-anonymity, PPRL, or PSI
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security game, theorem, reduction, DP, k-anonymity, or information-theoretic leakage measure
ZK in the paper means no named target, not zero-knowledge proof; fingerprint means behavioral cue pattern, not a hash
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TLS, TEE, PSI, PPRL, or secure computation
PPRL/PSI, DP aggregation, purpose-bound capability tokens are our inference and would require a different architecture
evidence_refs: pp.14-18 appendices A-F, including prompts and judge details

title: Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security
threat_model_summary: A malicious user submits adversarial task instructions to a multi-agent system; the attacker does not modify model weights or system code and interacts only through natural language and standard tool outputs. Only direct misuse is studied; indirect injection, memory poisoning, and adversarial agents are out of scope.
core_contributions: Adapts BrowserART, OS-Harm, and RedCode-Gen from single-agent to multi-agent evaluation
Controlled comparison of 13 architecture configurations along roles, topology, and memory across three environments and six models
Introduces stagewise metrics PR/ER/HA/HT plus benign success to separate planning refusal, execution interception, partial harm, and attack completion
Finds no universally safer architecture; BrowserART harmful-task completion rises from 10.0% standalone to 38.0% (3.8x) with benign accuracy not dropping
Releases all three benchmark adaptations and prompts
limitations: Static, non-adaptive attack prompts; HT should be read as a lower bound under adaptive attacks
Single run per configuration; no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests
OS-Harm benign success is near zero, so capability cost is not measurable there
No guardrail, monitor, or policy-checking baseline
Only three benchmarks and 13 configurations; no hierarchical, debate, or A2A/MCP architectures
Several internal numeric inconsistencies (RedCode benign 48 vs '54-56%', GPT-5.4 <=3% scope, Qwen3-VL benign range)
theoretical_crypto_links: None; PR/ER/HA/HT are benchmark stages, not security-game advantages
'Safety does not compose' is an empirical claim, not a composition theorem
Byzantine consensus and secure coordination are cited only as background, not used
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, TLS, signatures, credentials, TEE, or capability tokens
Capability tokens and signed delegation chains are our inference; the threat model is authorized-user misuse, so authentication is largely orthogonal

title: Position: Trustworthy Model Context Protocol Enables Responsible Agentic AI!
pdf_path: papers/Position_Trustworthy Model Context Protocol Enables Responsible Agentic AI!.pdf
threat_model_summary: No formal threat model. The paper cites typosquatting, tool poisoning, rug pulls, indirect prompt injection, and supply-chain compromise, but assumes a trusted host that can enforce consent and least privilege. Adversarial host compromise and network attackers are not modeled.
core_contributions: Analyzes MCP through the EU Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI
Identifies five intervention points: risk-adaptive requirements, metadata standardization, host enforcement, registry governance, and sustainability/fairness operationalization
Proposes Server Cards, minimal audit records, a redress interface, Eco Mode, and reference host requirements
Argues trustworthiness should shift from optional application features to protocol/ecosystem-level requirements
limitations: Position paper with no threat model, formal properties, protocol fields, implementation, or experiments
Host is assumed trusted and capable of enforcement, although the host is itself a prompt-injection surface
Server Cards are self-declared and not cryptographically verifiable
No wire-format, schema, state machine, conformance test, or reference implementation
Abstract promises 'fundamental shifts' that are not explicitly delivered as a numbered analysis
Citation inconsistencies (UNESCO attributed to Zhu et al. 2025; Commission 2020 vs 2019 Guidelines)
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security definition, game, construction, theorem, or reduction
'Trustworthy' is an ethical/legal/governance notion, not a cryptographic security property
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, TLS design, X.509, VC, signatures, TEE/attestation, ZK, or audit-log cryptography
Notes that MCP registries lack cryptographic validation, but proposes no cryptographic mechanism; signed Server Cards and transparency logs are our inference
evidence_refs: pp.1-2 motivation, MCP roles, five intervention points
p.3 registry trust gap and threats
pp.4-8 seven principles and concrete artifacts
p.9 alternative views, call to action, conclusion

title: AgentLAB: Benchmarking LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Attacks
pdf_path: papers/AgentLAB_Benchmarking LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Attacks.pdf
threat_model_summary: Two adversaries: a user adversary that replaces prompts (intent hijacking, tool chaining), and an environment adversary that injects content into observations (objective drifting, task injection, memory poisoning). Attacks unfold over multiple turns; black-box and white-box (CoT access) variants are considered. Malicious tasks target nine risk categories.
core_contributions: First benchmark dedicated to adaptive, long-horizon attacks on LLM agents
Five attack types across 28 environments and 644 security test cases
Planner-attacker-judge framework with TextGrad and memory bank; verifier for tool chaining
Evaluates six agents and finds overall ASR 28.9-81.5%; tool chaining 73.3-96.3%
Shows single-turn defenses transfer poorly; judge validation with 300 human-labeled examples
limitations: Simplified, reproducible environments may not reflect production noise and tool failures
Only five attack families; no multi-agent collusion or social-engineering chains
Attacker model differs by attack (Qwen3-14B-Abliterated vs GPT-5.1), confounding cross-attack ASR
No benign utility or over-refusal measurement
Judge matrix (TN/FN/FP/TP) contradicts reported FPR/FNR; Overall GPT-5.1 ASR does not match the five-category mean
System-level agents such as Claude Code and Codex are not covered
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security game, advantage, theorem, reduction, or cryptographic primitive
ASR is an empirical rate, not a cryptographic advantage; LLM judge is not an oracle
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, TLS, VC, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed tool-output provenance, capability gateways, and memory audit logs are our inference; they cannot decide whether a legitimately signed instruction is malicious
evidence_refs: p.1 abstract and five attack types
pp.3-6 threat model, benchmark design, Table 2
pp.7-8 single-turn vs long-horizon, defenses, Figures 7-8
